entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ageladas (or Hagelaedas), an eminent Argive sculptor, flourished in the pivotal period spanning the latter part of the 6th and the early 5th century BCE, marking a crucial transition from the Archaic to the Early Classical style in Greek art. Hailing from Argos, a city-state renowned for its athletic tradition and a distinct sculptural school, Ageladas stood as a leading figure, whose workshop not only produced significant works but also served as a crucible for the next generation of master sculptors. His significance lies not only in his own artistic output but profoundly in his role as a mentor to titans like Pheidias, Myron, and possibly Polykleitos, thereby directly influencing the zenith of Classical Greek sculpture.

His known commissions illustrate the artistic demands of his era and his mastery of bronze. Among his most celebrated works were the bronze statues of Olympic victors, including Kleosthenes of Epidamnus (c. 508 BCE) and Timasitheos of Delphi (c. 510 BCE), commissioned for the sanctuary at Olympia. He also created monumental cult statues, such as the bronze Zeus Ithomatas for the Messenians, established in their sanctuary on Mount Ithome around 460 BCE, and a statue of a Tarentine horse, possibly a dedication to the Delphian Apollo. These works, while largely lost, are attested by ancient authors like Pausanias, who consistently praised Ageladas’s skill in capturing anatomical realism and dynamic pose, moving beyond the rigid conventions of earlier periods.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ageladas holds significant historical importance as a master sculptor who bridged the Archaic and Early Classical periods, but even more so as the teacher of monumental figures like Pheidias and Myron, thereby directly shaping the trajectory of High Classical Greek sculpture and its enduring legacy.
